title: Kenosis: Christ Emptied Himself
lead: Kenosis, from the Greek verb in Philippians 2:7, 'he emptied himself', names the self-giving of the Son of God in becoming human and going to the cross, and the long debate over what that emptying meant.

sections.b: Philippians 2:6-11 tells how Christ, 'being in the form of God', did not count equality with God as something to exploit, emptied himself, took a slave's form, and was obedient to death on a cross; that is why God raised him and gave him the name above every name. Ernst Lohmeyer (1928) first set it out as a poem, and many think it is older than Paul.

The same downward movement appears elsewhere: 'He was rich, and yet he became poor for your sake' (2 Corinthians 8:9); Jesus set aside his outer clothes and washed his disciples' feet (John 13:4-5); 'He came to serve, and to give his life as a ransom in place of many' (Mark 10:45). Isaiah's servant 'emptied out his life to the point of death' (Isaiah 53:12).

In the nineteenth century Gottfried Thomasius, and later Charles Gore, P. T. Forsyth and H. R. Mackintosh, proposed that the Son limited some divine attributes in becoming human. Critics answer from the Chalcedonian confession of two natures 'unconfusedly, unchangeably, indivisibly, inseparably', and Pius XII condemned the kenotic doctrine in 1951 as 'a wicked invention' (Sempiternus Rex Christus 29). The Lutheran Formula of Concord and Calvin read the emptying as the concealing or non-use of the divine majesty, not its loss.
